items.title: 10 Things You Should Know About the Inheritance Talk
items.summary:
More than $120 trillion will pass between generations over the next two decades. Members of the baby boomer and Silent generations managed to accumulate unprecedented amounts of wealth as the stock market became more accessible, homeownership and home values rose, and retirement tools like 401(k)s and IRAs turned workers into long-term savers and investors. 

But as bank accounts and net worths swelled, Americans didn't all suddenly become comfortable talking about money. 

Kiplinger commissioned Morning Consult to conduct a survey to better understand Americans' feelings and beliefs about inheritance , including how prepared they feel – and how prepared they actually are. The survey reached 2,500 adult children (ages 25-60) with at least one living parent and 2,500 people aged 55+ with at least one adult child. Our research uncovered many potential problems in families' futures, many of which could be solved with open, ongoing conversation. 

Here are 10 things we learned:

1. More parents plan to leave an inheritance than children expect one Our research showed there's already a disconnect at a very basic level of understanding. Nearly 50% of the parent generation said they plan to leave a meaningful inheritance, but only 24% of children are expecting one. 

Additionally, there's a disconnect in expectations of what makes up parents' estates. Half of parents said traditional or Roth IRAs and 401(k)s are in their estate, but only a third of the younger generation said they believe that's in their parents' estate. Moreover, 54% of parents said real estate is in their…
items.t: 10 Things You Should Know About the Inheritance Talk

items.title: How to Cure Financial FOMO With the 48-Hour Rule
items.summary:
It's easier than ever to start comparing our lives to thousands of others at the touch of a button. 

Log in to any social media platform of your choice and you're bound to see someone post about buying a home or car, getting married, taking a dream vacation or even retiring . Or, a company or influencer will be trying to sell you a product or service. 

All of that exposure can make it feel like you have to make the purchase or do the thing to keep up, but over time, those feelings can come at a financial cost.

If you've felt financial FOMO , the financial fear of missing out, you're far from alone. Four in five Americans say the financial situations of people close to them have influenced how they view their own finances, according to a 2026 survey from the CFP Board . 

Last year, 51% of U.S. adults made an investment or purchase because of financial FOMO, according to a survey from Empower .

Although these feelings are common, spending more than you can afford to avoid the fear of missing out can quickly become a problem. 

I know because I did it.

items.title: Tax-Smart Strategies for Charitable Giving
items.summary:
Most of us give from the heart. And as icing on the cake, getting a tax deduction for your charitable contributions is a nice reward for your generosity. In recent years, however, those who claimed the standard deduction on their tax return — the majority of taxpayers — had to be satisfied with a thank-you note from the charities they supported, because only taxpayers who itemized could deduct their contributions. 

That will change, starting this year. A provision in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act will allow taxpayers who claim the standard deduction to deduct some of their charitable contributions. Another provision could encourage more taxpayers to itemize, enabling them to deduct even more of their contributions. 

But the OBBBA contains some downsides for givers, too. The law places a new limit on the amount itemizers can deduct, and it imposes additional restrictions on philanthropists who are in the top tax bracket. 

That doesn’t mean you should cut back on your giving. You’ll just need to be more strategic to get the most value for your charitable contributions. Look at it this way: Lowering your tax bill as much as possible now will give you that much more money to donate next year. 

And there’s no shortage of worthwhile organizations that need help.

Make the most of new rules. Starting with the 2026 tax year, taxpayers who claim the standard deduction can deduct up to $1,000 in cash donations to charities, or up to $2,000 for married couples who file jointly. 

This is significant because since the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act nearly doubled the standard…
items.t: Tax-Smart Strategies for Charitable Giving

items.title: How the Stock Market Has Changed Since the 1980s
items.summary:
Michael Mauboussin is head of consilient research at Counterpoint Global , an active fundamental equity team at Morgan Stanley Investment Management. He spent 40 years on Wall Street and more than three decades teaching investment analysis at Columbia Business School. In that time, he has worked with, taught and studied many great investors. 

Here, Kiplinger shares an excerpt from his latest book, The Investing Mind: A Guide to the Principles and Processes of Successful Investing , which was released on November 24. 

I have spent most of my time since the turn of the 21st century thinking about the process of investing. This includes topics such as market efficiency (where and how price and value diverge), valuation, competitive strategy analysis, and decision-making.

(Image credit: Harriman House / Pan Macmillan) We know substantially more about each of these areas today than we did in 1986, but there remains a vast amount to learn. I like to tell my students that this is an exciting time to be an investor because much of what we teach in business schools is a work in progress.

There has been enormous change in recent decades. Transaction costs have plummeted, with most individual investors now able to trade for free and institutions for pennies. items.title: How to Realistically Manage an Exit From Your Business
items.summary:
Most business owners I meet have a number in mind. It's what they believe their company could sell for someday: $5 million, $10 million, perhaps considerably more.

While they know this number, they often haven't calculated what they need from the business to fund the next stage of their lives. That's usually a very different sum.

An owner may believe selling your business for $6 million means having $6 million in cash available for retirement. But taxes, debt, transaction expenses, deal structure and other factors can significantly reduce what ultimately becomes investable wealth.

And that's only part of the equation.

For many entrepreneurs, the company is not simply an asset. It may pay their salary, provide distributions, cover health insurance, vehicles and travel, and fund other expenses that will eventually move from the company balance sheet to their personal one.

That's why I believe business owners should approach an exit from two directions at once: 

What is the business likely to be worth, and what does my life require it to be worth?

items.title: Is Your Financial Adviser Using AI and Your Data Safely?
items.summary:
Producing a polished explanation of a complex financial topic has become easier. Artificial intelligence (AI) can summarize research, organize information and draft an email in seconds. But deciding whether that explanation is accurate and useful still takes human work.

For a financial practice, it could be tempting to measure progress by how much faster things get done. Investors generally have a more practical interest: That the service helps them understand their choices and make informed decisions.

In my work with financial professionals, I view technology through the lens of the person receiving the service. If an AI tool helps a practice work faster, what improves for you? Better preparation, clearer explanations and more thoughtful follow-through are useful places to start.

Used responsibly, it can strengthen the preparation and communication behind a financial relationship. Its usefulness depends on someone knowing what to do with the output, including when to question it .

Put better preparation to work Some of the most practical applications are straightforward. FINRA's 2026 regulatory oversight report points out that summarizing documents and extracting information are the leading generative AI use cases among its member firms. Drafting content and automating workflows are other documented uses.

Within approved procedures, a financial professional could use AI to organize public research, develop a general meeting agenda or prepare an initial explanation of a financial concept. Each still needs review before it informs a discussion or reaches you.

items.title: Can the Fed Tackle Stubborn Inflation?
items.summary:
To help you understand what is going on in the economy our highly experienced Kiplinger Letter team will keep you abreast of the latest developments and forecasts ( Get a free issue of The Kiplinger Letter or subscribe ). Inflation is too high. You know it. We know it. The question: When will it get under control? And what will it take to achieve that? After five years of inflation exceeding the Federal Reserve’s goal of 2%, what must the Fed do to rein it in, and at what cost? 

Inflation, now near 4%, can get down to 3%, we think. The gradually higher interest rates the Fed is preparing to implement should help a bit. So will the calendar, as the year-over-year comparison the government uses to calculate inflation each month stops being worsened by this year’s energy price spike. Fuel prices will still be high next spring, but not higher than they were 12 months earlier. That effect alone will yield some good monthly inflation reports. 2027 may even sport a benign headline inflation rate.

items.title: Social Security Is Ditching 'Full Retirement Age'
items.summary:
Social Security's benefit formulas aren't changing, but the words the government uses to describe them are. Under the bipartisan Claiming Age Clarity Act , signed into law on November 20, 2026, the Social Security Administration (SSA) will scrap confusing legacy terms like " full retirement age " and " delayed retirement credits " in favor of plain-English labels that spell out exactly what your filing age does to your monthly check.

"Deciding when to claim Social Security is one of the biggest financial choices a senior will ever make. That choice should not hinge on government jargon that hides how much money is at stake. Thanks to the Claiming Age Clarity Act, Americans will now see plainly what they gain by waiting and what they give up by claiming their Social Security benefits early," said Ways and Means Committee Chairman Jason Smith (MO-08) in a press release . 

Changing a few words on a federal form won't solve Social Security's long-term funding challenges or magically expand anyone's nest egg. What it can do is strip away bureaucratic euphemisms at the exact moment workers are deciding when to file — ensuring that anyone who claims at 62 knows they are choosing the minimum monthly check, and anyone who holds out until 70 knows they are capturing the maximum.

Using "plain language" The Claiming Age Clarity Act ( H.R. 5284 ), sponsored by Reps. Lloyd Smucker (R-PA) and Don Beyer (D-VA) , updates the official terminology the SSA uses to describe retirement claiming ages, without changing benefit formulas, eligibility rules or payout amounts.

items.title: Is Anthropic's IPO the Peak of the AI Boom?
items.summary:

By the time the U.S. markets closed on November 20, ANT shares had retreated to about $89, giving back much of the post-IPO gains. Now, it's trading at about $87.

Was this "peak AI"? Impossible to tell. And a few trading days cannot provide adequate data. The more important question is whether investors are confusing a revolutionary technology with an investment that can succeed at any price.

History offers two lessons.

The dot-com lesson: Being right about technology is not enough In March 2000, the Nasdaq Composite peaked amid extraordinary optimism about the internet. By October 2002, it had fallen nearly 78% .

The internet did not fail. It transformed commerce and communication. But many investors assumed that every company connected to it would prosper, regardless of profits or valuation.

items.title: High-Yield Bond ETFs Pay More Income, But Taxes and Risk Can Take a Bite
items.summary:
As an asset class, bonds generally carry less risk than stocks. The trade-off is they offer lower potential returns. The reasoning comes down to the fundamental difference between equity and debt.

Stocks represent ownership in a company. As a shareholder, you participate in its potential growth through share price appreciation and, where applicable, dividends. But equity holders are also first in line to absorb losses. If a company goes bankrupt and its assets are liquidated, bondholders have a higher claim on whatever value remains, while shareholders receive anything left over.

Bondholders, meanwhile, are lenders. Even if the issuing company performs exceptionally well, their contractual upside is generally limited to receiving scheduled interest payments, known as coupons, and the return of principal at maturity. A more predictable payment structure plus higher priority in bankruptcy help explain why bonds typically offer lower expected returns than equities.

However, certain segments of the bond universe can offer yields that rival those of stocks. One prominent example is high-yield bonds, also known as non-investment-grade bonds or junk bonds . These are rated below BBB- by S&P Global Ratings and Fitch, or below Baa3 by Moody's. 

Such ratings indicate greater credit risk, including a higher likelihood that the issuer could experience financial distress or default. To compensate investors for taking on that additional uncertainty, these bonds typically offer higher yields than investment-grade debt.

Some companies issue bonds with non-investment-grade ratings…
items.t: High-Yield Bond ETFs Pay More Income, But Taxes and Risk Can Take a Bite

Cash savings A top priority is reviewing your cash savings because interest rates are competitive now. Look at your cash savings and divide them into three buckets:

Operating cash. These are the funds you use day to day to cover expenses. Typically, this is going to be in an easy-to-access checking account.

items.title: Got an IRMAA Predetermination Notice? You Have 10 Days to Act
items.summary:
When you enroll in Medicare for the first time , you expect to see standard monthly premiums for Part B and Part D. Instead, if IRS tax records show that your income from two years ago exceeded federal thresholds, you will first receive an IRMAA Predetermination Notice from the Social Security Administration (SSA) — a warning sent before your higher surcharge is formally locked in.

Unlike existing beneficiaries who receive IRMAA Determination Notices in the fall, new Medicare enrollees whose IRS records contain incomplete data, pending tax changes or filing status ambiguities get this advance notice first when they first apply for benefits . Fortunately, there is a 10-day window to verify or clarify the tax data Social Security plans to use before your initial premium is finalized. 

Here is why Social Security sends this notice, what is inside and how the timeline works.

4 common triggers of predetermination notices 

(Image credit: Getty Images) When existing Medicare beneficiaries are liable for the income-related monthly adjustment amount ( IRMAA ) during Social Security’s annual fall recalculation — and their IRS tax data is complete — they receive an official Initial Determination Notice . 

But new Medicare enrollees whose IRS records contain missing or irregular information go through a two-step process instead. A predetermination notice is only triggered when SSA’s system detects specific conditions or red flags during the IRS data match that require clarification.

Social Security issues this advance "notice of planned action" specifically when its automated…
items.t: Got an IRMAA Predetermination Notice? You Have 10 Days to Act

At most law schools , faculty have limited experience practicing law and dealing with clients, especially clients from all over the world. This affects their view of the attorney-client relationship.

In our multicultural country, lawyers newly admitted to the bar often discover a different world than they assumed, as "Catherine" from Cleveland described when she reached out to me.

"I recently opened my own law practice after working for a small estate planning law firm for about a year," she wrote in an email. "I am having problems with one of my clients.

"He is a physician, not originally from the United States, and even though we have a signed retainer agreement, he mailed a check for half the amount along with a note that said, 'I am paying for what I feel is warranted.' 

"I discovered that his prior lawyer had a similar experience with him and got out of the case that I am now handling. We are in the middle of a complicated litigation where he has been sued for non-payment of a lease he cosigned.

"I ignored a red flag that was apparent during our first meeting. When I told him that I could see no viable defense and that if the case went to trial, he would most likely lose and be required to pay the other side's attorney's fees and court costs, he nodded in apparent agreement, but then waved his hand and said, 'Don't worry. They will negotiate half of what they are suing for.'

items.title: Weigh In: Which Money Moment Had the Biggest Impact Over the Last 80 Years?
items.summary:
When Kiplinger Personal Finance debuted in 1947, a gallon of gas cost less than a quarter, credit cards weren't widely available and the internet was decades away.

Over the past 80 years, we've witnessed remarkable advances in technology, historic economic shifts, cultural milestones and events that changed the way we live, work and manage our money.

In celebration of our 80th anniversary , we're looking back at some of the most memorable moments across generations. Which one stands out to you? Cast your vote in the poll at the bottom of this article and let us know which milestone you remember most.

The Silent Generation (1928–1945) 

(Image credit: Getty Images) For the Silent Generation, the years following World War II brought economic growth and a changing way of life. Families moved to the suburbs, homeownership expanded and televisions became a fixture in living rooms across the country.

The introduction of the first modern credit card in 1950 changed how Americans paid for purchases, while the polio vaccine, introduced in 1955, marked a major public health breakthrough. These milestones helped shape a new era of prosperity, convenience and opportunity.

Baby boomers (1946–1964) 

(Image credit: Getty Images) Baby boomers grew up during a period of social change and historic achievements. The civil rights movement brought sweeping changes to laws and attitudes around racial equality, while the 1969 moon landing captured the world's attention. At the same time, the Woodstock music festival became a symbol of a generation embracing music, freedom and cultural…

items.title: Should You Skip Black Friday?
items.summary:
If you've been watching the early Black Friday deals roll out and are feeling less than impressed by them, you're not crazy. A slate of studies have emerged that all have similar findings: As much as 33% of the deals offered on Black Friday last year were "fake" deals. 

That is, the deal price was either the same or even higher than the price the product was selling for throughout most of the year. The teams behind these studies expect to see similar misleading deals plaguing this year's Black Friday . 

So, with so many fake Black Friday deals lurking in all these sales, should you skip shopping altogether? Not necessarily. Even with so many misleading discounts, the majority of deals were still legitimate and this can be a great opportunity to cross a lot of names off of your gift list for the holiday season. You just need to plan your deal-hunting accordingly and learn how to spot the difference between real and fake deals. 

A third of Black Friday deals aren't really saving you money Visualping , a website tracking tool that monitors price drops and other page changes, tracked 1,500 products across multiple categories during Black Friday last year. The company will be doing the same this year. Of those 1,500 products, 33% were cheaper before Black Friday than they were during the sales event. 

And it wasn't just a little more expensive either. On average, according to Visualping, these "fake" Black Friday deals were 37% more expensive than the product's lowest observed price. 

Wallethub conducted a similar study comparing Black Friday deal prices on Amazon with the…
items.t: Should You Skip Black Friday?
